hook: Leave a bunch of limp celery in a glass of cold water overnight and by morning the stalks snap crisply. Sprinkle salt on a slug and it shrivels. Give a hospital patient pure water straight into a vein and their red blood cells start to burst. All three are the same event: water crossing membranes toward the side with more dissolved stuff.

options: Net movement of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.
Net movement of particles from where they are less concentrated to where they are more concentrated.
Movement of particles that requires ATP from the cell.
Movement of particles that happens only in living cells.
prereq.why: Random motion spreads particles out, so more of them move from crowded regions to scarce ones than the reverse, until they are evenly spread.

options: They are channel proteins that let water cross the membrane quickly.
They pump water into the cell using ATP.
They block water from crossing the membrane.
They carry sugars across the membrane in exchange for water.
prereq.why: Aquaporins are water channels. Some water slips through the bilayer, but aquaporins let it cross far faster, with no energy spent.

figure.caption: The same three solutions do different things to an animal cell, which has no wall, and a plant cell, which does. Arrows show the net movement of water.

chain.cause: Dissolved solutes hold water molecules around them, so a solution with more solute has fewer water molecules free to move.
chain.effect: That solution has a lower water potential: a lower tendency for water to leave it.

chain.cause: A membrane lets water through but holds back many solutes.
chain.effect: Water moves by osmosis from the side with higher water potential (fewer solutes, hypotonic) to the side with lower water potential (more solutes, hypertonic).

chain.cause: An animal cell in a hypotonic solution keeps gaining water, and nothing resists its swelling.
chain.effect: It swells and may burst; in a hypertonic solution it loses water and shrivels; in an isotonic solution it stays the same.

chain.cause: A plant cell gaining water swells against its cell wall, and the wall pushes back.
chain.effect: Pressure builds inside (turgor), raising the cell's water potential until net water entry stops: the cell is firm, not burst.

chain.cause: A plant cell in a hypertonic solution loses water.
chain.effect: Turgor drops (the cell goes flaccid), and with more loss the membrane pulls away from the wall: plasmolysis.

chain.cause: Organisms whose surroundings differ from their cells keep gaining or losing water.
chain.effect: They osmoregulate: contractile vacuoles bail water out, kidneys adjust how much water leaves, and cells control their solute levels.

ideas: Hypotonic, isotonic and hypertonic are comparisons. A solution is hypertonic to something. Always say what you are comparing.
Water moves toward more solute, which is the same as saying from higher to lower water potential.
Water potential: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Pure water in an open container is 0. Solutes make Ψs negative; pressure from a cell wall makes Ψp positive.
Only solutes that cannot cross the membrane set tonicity. A solute that crosses spreads out evenly and stops mattering.
Count particles, not molecules: salt (NaCl) splits into two ions, so it lowers water potential about twice as much as the same amount of sugar.

misconception.wrong: In osmosis, the solute moves from the concentrated side to the dilute side until the two sides are equal.
misconception.right: In osmosis it is water that moves, toward the side with more solute, because the membrane holds the solute back. Solutes that can cross simply diffuse; that is not osmosis.

summary: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a membrane toward the side with more non-crossing solute, from higher to lower water potential (Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; pure water in an open container is 0). Compared with a cell, a hypotonic solution makes it gain water, a hypertonic one makes it lose water, and an isotonic one causes no net change. Animal cells burst or shrivel; plant cells become turgid against their walls or plasmolyze. Organisms osmoregulate with contractile vacuoles, kidneys and control of their own solute levels.
